claim: Shorea laevis is a slow-growing species with a mean annual increment (MAI) of diameter at breast height (DBH) of 0.38 cm/year as measured over a 20-year period.
source: S. laevis is a slow-growing species (Widiyatno et al., 2014), with a mean annual increment (MAI) of diameter at breast height (DBH) of 0.38 cm/year (as measured over a 20-year period in n=2 individuals; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements taken over 20 years and cited from Widiyatno et al., 2014.

claim: Shorea leprosula exhibits a faster growth rate with an MAI of 1.21 cm/year, which is 3.2 times greater than that of S. laevis.
source: In contrast, S. leprosula exhibits a faster growth rate (Widiyatno et al., 2014), with an MAI of 1.21 cm/year (n=18; Supplementary file 1a), which is 3.2 times greater than that of S. laevis.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth measurements and cited from Widiyatno et al., 2014.

claim: The average heights of the slow- and fast-growing species were 44.1 m and 43.9 m, respectively.
source: The average heights of the slow- and fast-growing species were 44.1 m and 43.9 m, respectively (Figure 1a; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct measurements reported in the manuscript.

claim: The average age of the slow-growing species was approximately 256 years.
source: While it is challenging to accurately estimate the age of tropical trees due to the absence of annual rings, we used the DBH/MAI to approximate the average age of the slow-growing species to be 256 years and the fast-growing species to be 66 years (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using DBH/MAI ratio, which is an inference from measured data.

claim: The average age of the fast-growing species was approximately 66 years.
source: While it is challenging to accurately estimate the age of tropical trees due to the absence of annual rings, we used the DBH/MAI to approximate the average age of the slow-growing species to be 256 years and the fast-growing species to be 66 years (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using DBH/MAI ratio, which is an inference from measured data.

claim: The genomes of S. laevis and S. leprosula were estimated to contain 52,935 and 40,665 protein-coding genes, respectively.
source: The genomes were estimated to contain 52,935 and 40,665 protein-coding genes, covering 97.9% and 97.8% of complete BUSCO genes (eudicots_odb10) for the slow- and fast-growing species (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome assembly and annotation data.

claim: The genomes of S. laevis and S. leprosula covered 97.9% and 97.8% of complete BUSCO genes (eudicots_odb10), respectively.
source: The genomes were estimated to contain 52,935 and 40,665 protein-coding genes, covering 97.9% and 97.8% of complete BUSCO genes (eudicots_odb10) for the slow- and fast-growing species (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by BUSCO analysis of genome completeness.

claim: Genome sizes estimated using k-mer distribution were 347 and 376 Mb for the slow- and fast-growing species, respectively.
source: Genome sizes estimated using k-mer distribution were 347 and 376 Mb for the slow- and fast-growing species, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by k-mer analysis of sequencing data.

claim: The synteny relationship between S. laevis and S. leprosula exhibited a high level of conservation overall.
source: The synteny relationship between S. laevis and S. leprosula exhibited a high level of conservation overall (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by synteny analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A total of 64 DNA samples were sequenced, yielding an average coverage of 69.3 and 56.5×per sample for the slow- and fast-growing species, respectively.
source: A total of 64 DNA samples were sequenced, yielding an average coverage of 69.3 and 56.5×per sample for the slow- and fast-growing species, respectively (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data reported in the manuscript.

claim: 728 and 234 SNVs were identified in S1 and S2, respectively.
source: We identified 728 and 234 SNVs in S1 and S2, and 106 and 68 SNVs in F1 and F2, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by SNV calling from sequencing data.

claim: 106 and 68 SNVs were identified in F1 and F2, respectively.
source: We identified 728 and 234 SNVs in S1 and S2, and 106 and 68 SNVs in F1 and F2, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by SNV calling from sequencing data.

claim: All somatic mutations were unique and did not overlap between individuals.
source: All somatic mutations were unique and did not overlap between individuals.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of SNV data across individuals.

claim: Amplicon sequencing demonstrated accurate annotation for 31 out of 33 mutations (94% overall), with 22 out of 24 mutations on S1 and all 9 mutations on S2.
source: Our analysis demonstrated accurate annotation for 31 out of 33 mutations (94% overall), with 22 out of 24 mutations on S1 and all 9 mutations on S2 (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by independent validation using amplicon sequencing.

claim: Phylogenetic trees constructed using somatic mutations were almost perfectly congruent with the physical tree structures.
source: Phylogenetic trees constructed using somatic mutations were almost perfectly congruent with the physical tree structures (Figure 1a), even though we did not incorporate knowledge of the branching topology of the tree in the SNV discovery process.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of phylogenetic trees with physical tree structures shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The number of SNVs increases linearly as the physical distance between branch tips increases.
source: Our analysis revealed that the number of SNVs increases linearly as the physical distance between branch tips increases (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per meter was 7.08×10–9 (95% CI: 6.41–7.74×10−9) for S1.
source: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per meter was 7.08×10–9 (95% CI: 6.41–7.74×10−9) and 4.27×10–9 (95% CI: 3.99–4.55×10−9) for S1 and S2, and 1.77×10–9 (95% CI: 1.64–1.91×10−9) and 1.29×10–9 (95% CI: 1.05–1.53×10−9) for F1 and F2, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis of SNV accumulation with distance.

claim: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per meter was 4.27×10–9 (95% CI: 3.99–4.55×10−9) for S2.
source: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per meter was 7.08×10–9 (95% CI: 6.41–7.74×10−9) and 4.27×10–9 (95% CI: 3.99–4.55×10−9) for S1 and S2, and 1.77×10–9 (95% CI: 1.64–1.91×10−9) and 1.29×10–9 (95% CI: 1.05–1.53×10−9) for F1 and F2, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis of SNV accumulation with distance.

claim: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per meter was 1.77×10–9 (95% CI: 1.64–1.91×10−9) for F1.
source: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per meter was 7.08×10–9 (95% CI: 6.41–7.74×10−9) and 4.27×10–9 (95% CI: 3.99–4.55×10−9) for S1 and S2, and 1.77×10–9 (95% CI: 1.64–1.91×10−9) and 1.29×10–9 (95% CI: 1.05–1.53×10−9) for F1 and F2, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis of SNV accumulation with distance.

claim: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per meter was 1.29×10–9 (95% CI: 1.05–1.53×10−9) for F2.
source: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per meter was 7.08×10–9 (95% CI: 6.41–7.74×10−9) and 4.27×10–9 (95% CI: 3.99–4.55×10−9) for S1 and S2, and 1.77×10–9 (95% CI: 1.64–1.91×10−9) and 1.29×10–9 (95% CI: 1.05–1.53×10−9) for F1 and F2, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis of SNV accumulation with distance.

claim: The average rate of somatic mutation for the slow-growing species was 5.67×10–9 nucleotide–1 m–1, which is 3.7-fold higher than the average rate of 1.53×10–9 nucleotide–1 m–1 observed in the fast-growing species.
source: The average rate of somatic mutation for the slow-growing species was 5.67×10–9 nucleotide–1 m–1, which is 3.7-fold higher than the average rate of 1.53×10–9 nucleotide–1 m–1 observed in the fast-growing species (Figure 2b; Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of mutation rates calculated from the data.

claim: The length and diameter of fiber cells in both species are not substantially different: 1.29 mm and 19.0 μm for the slow-growing species and 0.91 mm and 22.7 μm for the fast-growing species.
source: This cannot be explained by differences in the number of cell divisions, as the length and diameter of fiber cells in both species are not substantially different 1.29 mm and 19.0 μm for the slow-growing species (Usami, 1978) and 0.91 mm and 22.7 μm for the fast-growing species (Praptoyo and Mayaningsih, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited measurements from Usami, 1978 and Praptoyo and Mayaningsih, 2012.

claim: The somatic mutation rate per nucleotide per year was on average 7.71×10–10 for the slow-growing species and 8.05×10–10 for the fast-growing species.
source: On average, resultant values were largely similar between the two species, with 7.71×10–10 and 8.05×10–10 nucleotide–1 year–1 for the slow- and fast-growing species, respectively (Figure 2b; Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations based on estimated tree age and mutation accumulation.

claim: Somatic mutation accumulates in a clock-like manner as trees age regardless of tree growth.
source: This result suggests that somatic mutation accumulates in a clock-like manner as they age regardless of tree growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutation rates per year are similar between species with different growth rates.

claim: Estimates of somatic mutation rates per nucleotide per year in Shorea are higher than those previously reported in other long-lived trees such as Quercus robur, Populus trichocarpa, Eucalyptus melliodora, and Picea sitchensis.
source: Our estimates of somatic mutation rates per nucleotide per year in Shorea are higher than those previously reported in other long-lived trees such as Quercus robur (Schmid-Siegert et al., 2017), Populus trichocarpa (Hofmeister et al., 2020), Eucalyptus melliodora (Orr et al., 2020), and Picea sitchensis (Hanlon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited studies on other tree species.

claim: The mutational spectra showed a dominance of cytosine-to-thymine (C>T and G>A on the other strand) substitutions at CpG sites.
source: Across species, the mutational spectra showed a dominance of cytosine-to-thymine (C>T and G>A on the other strand, noted as C:G>T:A) substitutions at CpG sites with CG (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutational spectrum analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The dominance of C>T substitutions at CpG sites is believed to result from the spontaneous deamination of 5-methylcytosine.
source: This is believed to result from the spontaneous deamination of 5-methylcytosine (Coulondre et al., 1978; Duncan and Miller, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on the mechanism of C>T mutations.

claim: The proportion of somatic mutations at CpG sites showed a 3.38-fold and 2.56-fold increase for F1 and F2, and a 4.54-fold and 3.53-fold increase for S1 and S2, respectively, compared to the proportion of CpG sites in the reference genomes.
source: Compared to the proportion of CpG sites in the reference genomes, the proportion of somatic mutations at CpG sites showed a 3.38-fold and 2.56-fold increase for F1 and F2, and a 4.54-fold and 3.53-fold increase for S1 and S2, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of observed mutation frequencies with expected frequencies.

claim: The mutational spectra were largely similar to the dominant mutation signature in humans known as SBS1 (cosine similarity = 0.789 and 0.597 for the slow- and fast-growing species).
source: The mutational spectra were largely similar to the dominant mutation signature in humans known as SBS1 (cosine similarity = 0.789 and 0.597 for the slow- and fast-growing species; Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by cosine similarity analysis comparing tree mutations to human cancer signatures.

claim: SBS1 is believed to result from the spontaneous deamination of 5-methylcytosine.
source: SBS1 is believed to result from the spontaneous deamination of 5-methylcytosine.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about SBS1 signature.

claim: The mutational spectra were also comparable to another dominant signature in all human cancers, SBS5 (cosine similarity = 0.577 and 0.558 for the slow- and fast-growing species).
source: The mutational spectra were also comparable to another dominant signature in all human cancers, SBS5 (cosine similarity = 0.577 and 0.558 for the slow- and fast-growing species; Supplementary file 1i), the origin of which remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by cosine similarity analysis comparing tree mutations to human cancer signatures.

claim: The origin of SBS5 remains unknown.
source: The mutational spectra were also comparable to another dominant signature in all human cancers, SBS5 (cosine similarity = 0.577 and 0.558 for the slow- and fast-growing species; Supplementary file 1i), the origin of which remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on current knowledge about SBS5 signature.

claim: Somatic mutations in tropical trees accumulate in a clock-like manner, which is consistent with the clock-like mutational process observed in SBS1 and SBS5 in human somatic cells.
source: Our finding that somatic mutations in tropical trees accumulate in a clock-like manner (Figure 2a) is consistent with the clock-like mutational process observed in SBS1 and SBS5 in human somatic cells (Alexandrov et al., 2015; Lee-Six et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited studies on human somatic mutations.

claim: The mutational processes in plants and animals are conserved, despite the variation in their life forms and environmental conditions.
source: This suggests that the mutational processes in plants and animals are conserved, despite the variation in their life forms and environmental conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity of mutational signatures between tropical trees and human cells.

claim: The observed rate of non-synonymous somatic mutations did not deviate significantly from the expected rate under the null hypothesis of neutral selection in both the slow- (binomial test: p=0.71) and fast-growing (binomial test: p=1.0) species.
source: The observed rate of non-synonymous somatic mutations did not deviate significantly from the expected rate under the null hypothesis of neutral selection in both the slow- (binomial test: p=0.71) and fast-growing (binomial test: p=1.0) species (Figure 4b; Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing of observed vs. expected mutation rates.

claim: The number of inter-individual SNVs were significantly smaller than expected (p<10–15 for both species).
source: In contrast, the number of inter-individual SNVs were significantly smaller than expected (p<10–15 for both species: Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing of observed vs. expected mutation rates.

claim: Somatic mutations are largely neutral within an individual.
source: These results indicate that somatic mutations are largely neutral within an individual, but mutations passed to next generation are subject to strong purifying selection during the process of embryogenesis, seed germination, and growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that non-synonymous somatic mutations do not deviate from neutral expectations.

claim: Mutations passed to next generation are subject to strong purifying selection during the process of embryogenesis, seed germination, and growth.
source: These results indicate that somatic mutations are largely neutral within an individual, but mutations passed to next generation are subject to strong purifying selection during the process of embryogenesis, seed germination, and growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that inter-individual SNVs show significantly fewer non-synonymous mutations than expected.

claim: The fraction of C>T substitutions, in particular at CpG sites, was lower in inter-individual SNVs compared to somatic SNVs.
source: However, the fraction of C>T substitutions, in particular at CpG sites, was lower in inter-individual SNVs compared to somatic SNVs (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of mutational spectra shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The lower fraction of C>T substitutions in inter-individual SNVs may be indicative of the potential influence of GC-biased gene conversion during meiosis or biased purifying selection for C>T inter-individual nucleotide substitutions.
source: This observation may be indicative of the potential influence of GC-biased gene conversion during meiosis (Duret and Galtier, 2009) or biased purifying selection for C>T inter-individual nucleotide substitutions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing possible explanations for the observed pattern with citation support.

claim: The somatic mutation rate per meter is higher in the slow- than in fast-growing species.
source: Our study demonstrates that while the somatic mutation rate per meter is higher in the slow- than in fast-growing species, the somatic mutation rate per year is independent of growth rate.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The somatic mutation rate per year is independent of growth rate.
source: Our study demonstrates that while the somatic mutation rate per meter is higher in the slow- than in fast-growing species, the somatic mutation rate per year is independent of growth rate.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The replication dependent mutation emanates from errors that occur during DNA replication, such as the misincorporation of a nucleotide during DNA synthesis.
source: The replication dependent mutation emanates from errors that occur during DNA replication, such as the misincorporation of a nucleotide during DNA synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about DNA replication errors.

claim: The replication independent mutation arises from DNA damage caused by endogenous reactions or exogenous mutagens at any time of cell cycle.
source: The replication independent mutation arises from DNA damage caused by endogenous reactions or exogenous mutagens at any time of cell cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sources of DNA damage.

claim: The same number of cell divisions are required to achieve 1 m of growth in both species as the cell size is similar between the two species.
source: It is also reasonable to assume that the same number of cell divisions are required to achieve 1 m of growth in both species as the cell size is similar between the two species.
evidence: The claim is an assumption based on the observation that cell sizes are similar.

claim: The preponderance of non-replicative mutational process can be attributed to its distinct molecular origin, the accumulation of spontaneous CpG mutations with absolute time.
source: The preponderance of non-replicative mutational process can be attributed to its distinct molecular origin, the accumulation of spontaneous CpG mutations with absolute time.
evidence: The claim is an inference connecting the observed mutational patterns to the proposed mechanism.

claim: The neutral nature of newly arising somatic mutations within the tree results in a molecular clock, a constant rate of molecular evolution.
source: The neutral nature of newly arising somatic mutations within the tree results in a molecular clock, a constant rate of molecular evolution (Zuckerkandl and Pauling, 1965; Kimura and Ota, 1971; Kimura, 1983).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and cited molecular clock theory.

claim: The humid tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia are characterized by a preponderance of trees of the Dipterocarpaceae family.
source: The humid tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia are characterized by a preponderance of trees of the Dipterocarpaceae family (Ghazoul, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ghazoul, 2016.

claim: Dipterocarp trees are highly valued for both their contribution to forest diversity and their use in timber production.
source: Dipterocarp trees are highly valued for both their contribution to forest diversity and their use in timber production.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about Dipterocarp trees.

claim: The study site is located just below the equator in central Borneo, Indonesia.
source: We selected the two largest individuals of each species (S1 and S2 for S.laevis and F1 and F2 for S. leprosula; Figure 1a) at the study site, located just below the equator in central Borneo, Indonesia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description and map shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The mean annual temperature range from 2001–2009 was between 22 to 28°C at night and 30 to 33°C during the day, with an average annual precipitation of 3376 mm at the study site.
source: The mean annual temperature range from 2001–2009 was between 22 to 28°C at night and 30 to 33°C during the day, with an average annual precipitation of 3376 mm41.
evidence: The claim is supported by climate data for the study site.

claim: It is challenging to accurately estimate the age of tropical trees due to the absence of annual rings.
source: While it is challenging to accurately estimate the age of tropical trees due to the absence of annual rings, we used the DBH/MAI to approximate the average age of the slow-growing species to be 256 years and the fast-growing species to be 66 years (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about tropical tree biology.

claim: Genome sizes estimated using k-mer distribution were 8% and 7% smaller than the estimates obtained through flow cytometry for the slow- and fast-growing species, respectively.
source: Estimated genome sizes were 347 Mb for the slow-growing species and 376 Mb for the fast-growing species. These estimates were 8% and 7% smaller than the estimates obtained through flow cytometry (Ng et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited flow cytometry data.

claim: The genome size of the fast-growing species was nearly identical to that previously reported for S. leprosula in peninsular Malaysia.
source: The genome size of the fast-growing species was nearly identical to that previously reported for S. leprosula in peninsular Malaysia (Ng et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited data from Ng et al., 2021.

claim: The estimated percentages of the repetitive sequences were 42.4% for S. laevis and 39.5% for S. leprosula.
source: The estimated percentages of the repetitive sequences were 42.4% for S. laevis and 39.5% for S. leprosula (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by repeat masking analysis of the genomes.

claim: The sequence reads were mapped to the reference genome, yielding average mapping rates of 91.61% and 89.5% for the slow- and fast-growing species, respectively.
source: The sequence reads were mapped to the reference genome, yielding average mapping rates of 91.61% and 89.5% for the slow- and fast-growing species, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data analysis.

claim: 4% of the total SNVs (46/1136) were homozygous.
source: Most of the somatic SNVs were heterozygous, whereas 4% of the total SNVs (46/1136) were homozygous (Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of SNV data.

claim: The homozygous sites were treated as a single mutation due to the likelihood of a genotyping error being higher than the probability of two mutations occurring at the same site.
source: The homozygous sites were treated as a single mutation due to the likelihood of a genotyping error being higher than the probability of two mutations occurring at the same site.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the relative probabilities of genotyping error vs. recurrent mutation.

claim: A greater number of somatic mutations were identified in tropical trees than in temperate trees.
source: Using newly constructed genomes, we identified a greater number of somatic mutations in tropical trees than in temperate trees.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison with literature on temperate trees.

claim: A linear increase in the number of somatic mutations with physical distance between branches was observed in both species.
source: In both species, we observed a linear increase in the number of somatic mutations with physical distance between branches.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The rate of somatic mutation accumulation per meter of growth was 3.7-fold higher in S. laevis than in S. leprosula.
source: However, we found that the rate of somatic mutation accumulation per meter of growth was 3.7-fold higher in S. laevis than in S. leprosula.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The difference in the somatic mutation rate was scaled with the slower growth rate of S. laevis compared to S. leprosula, resulting in a constant somatic mutation rate per year between the two species.
source: This difference in the somatic mutation rate was scaled with the slower growth rate of S. laevis compared to S. leprosula, resulting in a constant somatic mutation rate per year between the two species.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Older trees have a greater contribution towards generating genetic variation.
source: These findings suggest that somatic mutations accumulate with absolute time and older trees have a greater contribution towards generating genetic variation.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the finding that mutations accumulate with time rather than growth.

claim: The rate of somatic mutations per year in a 234-year-old oak tree has been found to be surprisingly low compared to the rate in an annual herb.
source: The rate of somatic mutations per year in a 234-year-old oak tree has been found to be surprisingly low (Schmid-Siegert et al., 2017) compared to the rate in an annual her (Ossowski et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmid-Siegert et al., 2017 and Ossowski et al., 2010.

claim: Similar analyses in other long-lived trees have also shown low mutation rates in both broadleaf trees and conifers.
source: Similar analyses in other long-lived trees have also shown low mutation rates in both broadleaf trees (Plomion et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019; Orr et al., 2020; Hofmeister et al., 2020; Duan et al., 2022) and conifers (Hanlon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on tree mutation rates.

claim: There is currently no knowledge on the somatic mutation landscapes in organisms living in tropical ecosystems.
source: Despite the growing body of knowledge of somatic mutation landscapes in temperate regions, there is currently no knowledge on the somatic mutation landscapes in organisms living in tropical ecosystems, which are among the most diverse biomes on Earth.
evidence: The claim is based on review of existing literature.

claim: Tropical ecosystems are among the most diverse biomes on Earth.
source: Despite the growing body of knowledge of somatic mutation landscapes in temperate regions, there is currently no knowledge on the somatic mutation landscapes in organisms living in tropical ecosystems, which are among the most diverse biomes on Earth.
evidence: The claim is based on established ecological knowledge.

claim: Mutations can arise from errors during replication.
source: Mutations can arise from errors during replication (Reijns et al., 2015), or from DNA damage caused by exogenous mutagens or endogenous reactions at any time during cell growth (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reijns et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations can arise from DNA damage caused by exogenous mutagens or endogenous reactions at any time during cell growth.
source: Mutations can arise from errors during replication (Reijns et al., 2015), or from DNA damage caused by exogenous mutagens or endogenous reactions at any time during cell growth (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2016.

claim: DNA replication errors have long been assumed to be major sources of mutations.
source: While DNA replication errors have long been assumed to be major sources of mutations (Makova and Li, 2002; Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015), a modeling study that relates the mutation rate to rates of DNA damage, repair and cell division (Gao et al., 2016) and experimental studies in yeast (Liu and Zhang, 2019), human (Abascal et al., 2021), and other animals de Manuel et al., 2022 have shown the importance of mutagenic processes that do not depend on cell division.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Makova and Li, 2002 and Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015.

claim: A modeling study and experimental studies in yeast, human, and other animals have shown the importance of mutagenic processes that do not depend on cell division.
source: While DNA replication errors have long been assumed to be major sources of mutations (Makova and Li, 2002; Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015), a modeling study that relates the mutation rate to rates of DNA damage, repair and cell division (Gao et al., 2016) and experimental studies in yeast (Liu and Zhang, 2019), human (Abascal et al., 2021), and other animals de Manuel et al., 2022 have shown the importance of mutagenic processes that do not depend on cell division.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2016, Liu and Zhang, 2019, Abascal et al., 2021, and de Manuel et al., 2022.

claim: It remains largely unknown which source of mutations, whether replicative or non-replicative, predominates in naturally growing organisms.
source: Consequently, it remains largely unknown which source of mutations, whether replicative or non-replicative, predominates in naturally growing organisms.
evidence: The claim is based on review of existing knowledge gaps.

claim: Methylated CpG sites spontaneously deaminate, leading to TpG sites and increasing the number of C>T substitutions.
source: Methylated CpG sites spontaneously deaminate, leading to TpG sites and increasing the number of C>T substitutions (Cooper and Krawczak, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cooper and Krawczak, 1989.

claim: The clock-like mutational process is observed in SBS1 and SBS5 in human somatic cells.
source: Our finding that somatic mutations in tropical trees accumulate in a clock-like manner (Figure 2a) is consistent with the clock-like mutational process observed in SBS1 and SBS5 in human somatic cells (Alexandrov et al., 2015; Lee-Six et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alexandrov et al., 2015 and Lee-Six et al., 2019.
